lead: Optical flow is the apparent motion of brightness patterns between two video frames. It gives a vector (u, v) at each pixel: how far that pixel seems to move in one frame interval. The idea exists because true object motion is hidden, but brightness patterns are observable. Flow drives video compression, stabilisation, tracking, and driver-assistance systems. It is not the same as the motion field, the true 3D motion projected on the image. Textures, lighting and occlusion make the two differ.
prereq: You need: image gradients and convolution from Unit 2, the local window matrix from Harris corner detection, and basic linear algebra (2×2 matrix inverse).

sections.h3: Brightness constancy and the gradient equation

blocks.text: Let I(x, y, t) be brightness at pixel (x, y) at frame time t. A small pattern moves by u pixels in x and v pixels in y in one frame. Brightness constancy assumes the pattern keeps the same brightness: I(x + u, y + v, t + 1) = I(x, y, t). A first-order Taylor expansion gives I(x, y, t) + I<sub>x</sub>u + I<sub>y</sub>v + I<sub>t</sub> = I(x, y, t). Cancel I(x, y, t).

blocks.where: I<sub>x</sub> = ∂I/∂x and I<sub>y</sub> = ∂I/∂y are spatial brightness gradients; I<sub>t</sub> = ∂I/∂t is the change per frame; u and v are flow in pixels/frame.

blocks.text: One equation has two unknowns. At a single pixel we can only see motion along the brightness gradient. This is the aperture problem. A straight edge moved along itself looks unchanged, so motion along the edge is invisible. A corner has gradients in two directions and fixes both components.

Optical flow is not always the true motion field. A moving white wall has no texture, so flow is zero while the wall moves. Specular highlights and shadows also move differently from surfaces. Some syllabi call this motion estimation.

Lucas-Kanade assumes u and v are constant in a small window around the pixel. For each pixel i in the window: I<sub>xi</sub>u + I<sub>yi</sub>v = −I<sub>ti</sub>. Stack all rows into A d = b, where d = [u, v]<sup>T</sup>, row i of A is [I<sub>xi</sub>, I<sub>yi</sub>], and b is the column of −I<sub>ti</sub>.

blocks.where: A holds spatial gradients in the window; b holds negative temporal gradients; d = (u, v) is the flow in pixels/frame.

blocks.text: ATA is the same second-moment matrix used by Harris corners (5.1). It is invertible only when the window has gradients in two directions. Flat window: no solution. Straight edge: one reliable direction. Corner: both.

items: Compute I<sub>x</sub>, I<sub>y</sub> and I<sub>t</sub> by finite differences between frames.
For each pixel, sum I<sub>x</sub><sup>2</sup>, I<sub>x</sub>I<sub>y</sub>, I<sub>y</sub><sup>2</sup>, I<sub>x</sub>I<sub>t</sub> and I<sub>y</sub>I<sub>t</sub> over the window.
Solve the 2×2 normal equations for u and v.
For large motion, build an image pyramid: solve at the coarsest level, upsample the flow, and refine at finer levels (5.9).

blocks.text: Horn-Schunck adds a global smoothness assumption: neighbouring pixels should have similar flow. It minimises an energy with two terms.

blocks.where: the first term enforces brightness constancy; α is a positive smoothness weight; ∇u and ∇v are spatial gradients of the flow field; Σ runs over all pixels.

blocks.text: Only a few universities teach the full variational derivation. The result is an iterative update that fills flat regions but blurs flow at object boundaries. Lucas-Kanade is local and sparse; Horn-Schunck is global and dense. Pyramidal Lucas-Kanade with tracking is common for feature points. Dense variational methods are used when every pixel is needed.

items: Video compression: MPEG stores motion vectors for blocks.
Camera stabilisation and frame interpolation use flow to shift pixels.
Driver assistance uses flow to detect approaching objects.
Medical imaging uses flow to measure tissue motion between scans.

examples.question: Two pixels in a 2×2 window give brightness equations. Pixel A has (I<sub>x</sub>, I<sub>y</sub>, I<sub>t</sub>) = (2, 0, 1). Pixel B has (I<sub>x</sub>, I<sub>y</sub>, I<sub>t</sub>) = (0, 2, 1). Units are intensity per pixel and intensity per frame. Use Lucas-Kanade to find flow (u, v) in pixels/frame and its magnitude.
steps: Write the brightness equation for pixel A: 2u + 0v + 1 = 0.
Write the brightness equation for pixel B: 0u + 2v + 1 = 0.

import math
Ix1, Iy1, It1 = 2.0, 0.0, 1.0
Ix2, Iy2, It2 = 0.0, 2.0, 1.0
u = -It1 / Ix1
v = -It2 / Iy2
mag = math.sqrt(u*u + v*v)
print(u)
print(v)
print(round(mag, 3))

traps: Using one pixel equation for two unknowns: Ix u + Iy v + It = 0 alone cannot give both u and v unless one gradient is zero and you accept the other component as unknown.
Confusing optical flow with true object motion: a moving untextured wall gives zero flow, and a moving shadow gives flow where no surface moves.
Sign slip: from Ix u + Iy v + It = 0, a positive It with positive Ix gives negative u, not positive u.
Unit slip: u and v are pixels/frame; Ix is intensity per pixel, It is intensity per frame. Mixing frame steps scales the answer wrongly.
Using a small Lucas-Kanade window for large motion: the displacement leaves the window and the solution is wrong. Use a pyramid.

quiz.q: Write the brightness constancy equation and the resulting gradient equation. Define each symbol.
quiz.a: Brightness constancy: I(x + u, y + v, t + 1) = I(x, y, t). Gradient equation: Ix u + Iy v + It = 0, where Ix and Iy are spatial derivatives of brightness, It is the frame-to-frame derivative, and u, v are flow in pixels/frame.

quiz.q: Why can a single pixel not recover both flow components u and v?
quiz.a: The gradient equation is one linear equation in two unknowns. A single pixel only measures brightness change along its gradient direction, so motion along an edge is invisible. This is the aperture problem; a window with gradients in two directions is needed.

quiz.q: A pixel has Ix = 3, Iy = 0, It = 6, in intensity per pixel and intensity per frame. What can you determine about its flow?
quiz.a: Use 3u + 0v + 6 = 0, so u = −2 pixels/frame. v is unknown because Iy = 0. This is an aperture case: only the component across the vertical edge is visible.

quiz.q: Pixel A has (Ix, Iy, It) = (1, 1, 2). Pixel B has (1, −1, 0). Solve the two-pixel Lucas-Kanade system for (u, v).
quiz.a: Pixel A: u + v + 2 = 0 → u + v = −2. Pixel B: u − v + 0 = 0 → u = v. Substitute: 2u = −2 → u = −1, v = −1. Flow = (−1, −1) pixels/frame.

quiz.q: Why does an image pyramid help Lucas-Kanade estimate large motion?
quiz.a: A small window assumes constant flow nearby. Large motion leaves the window, so the linearisation fails. At a coarse pyramid level the same motion is only a few pixels, so the window succeeds. The coarse flow is upsampled and refined at finer levels.

quiz.q: Give two situations where brightness constancy fails and state the effect on optical flow.
quiz.a: Occlusion: a surface appears or disappears, so no matching brightness exists and flow is wrong near the boundary. Lighting change or specular highlight: brightness changes without surface motion, so It is large and the solver reports false motion. Other valid cases include shadows and transparent surfaces.

quiz.q: Compare Lucas-Kanade and Horn-Schunck in one short paragraph.
quiz.a: Lucas-Kanade is local: it solves a small window least-squares problem and usually gives sparse flow at corners. Horn-Schunck is global: it adds a smoothness penalty over the whole image and gives dense flow, but blurs boundaries and needs iteration.

beyond: Not for the exam. Deep networks such as FlowNet and RAFT learn flow directly from image pairs and now lead on public benchmarks. Event cameras and optical flow sensors use the same brightness-change idea at microsecond timing. Search terms: brightness constancy, Lucas-Kanade, Horn-Schunck, pyramidal flow, RAFT.
